On small held-out samples it beats static and random orderings on AG News but not on TREC. See highlights Open arxiv.org Format Article Reading time 2 min Published by Community Last verified Oct 2026 Tags community research arxiv cost uncertainty decision-models Works for Jev for Decision gating Jev for Scoring Jev for Evaluation Used in Jev for Data & Analytics Jev for Software & DevTools Highlights Aggregates path-dependent tree proposals, weights them by global training information gain, and labels with a shared masked classifier. Four-question forest acquisition reaches 0.729 on AG News (n=48) versus 0.667 static gain ranking and 0.583 random ordering. On TREC (n=24) the ordering reverses: forest 0.667 versus 0.750 and 0.833 for the alternatives. Batching all eight questions beats four sequential forest queries on accuracy, measured cost, and latency. Offline MiniBooNE reaches 0.845±0.010 at ten features and 0.885±0.008 at forty features. Watch out arXiv preprint posted October 7, 2026 (stat.ML, cs.LG) by Yu Yan. Samples are tiny (n=48 and n=24), and the author states the findings are exploratory and do not support a general path-voting advantage: value depends on the task, predictor, and whether budgets count questions or actual query costs. Questions about this entry Short answers drawn from the linked project or page. What is JevForest's feature-acquisition policy? JevForest aggregates path-dependent proposals from bootstrapped trees, weights them by global training information gain, and predicts from acquired values with a shared masked classifier; an online implementation queries Jev for the selected semantic answers. How does four-question forest acquisition do on AG News? It scores 0.729 accuracy on AG News (n=48), compared with 0.667 for a static gain ranking and 0.583 for random ordering. What happens to that ordering on TREC? The ordering reverses: forest accuracy is 0.667 on TREC (n=24), compared with 0.750 for static gain ranking and 0.833 for random ordering. Are batched questions cheaper than sequential ones here? Asking all eight questions in one batch yields higher accuracy at lower measured cost and latency than four sequential forest queries; direct Jev classification matches the batch accuracy while costing less. What do the offline MiniBooNE experiments show? Accuracy of 0.845±0.010 at ten features and 0.885±0.008 at forty features, reported over three jointly varying data and forest seeds as mean plus or minus sample standard deviation. Does the paper claim a general advantage for path voting? No. The author frames the results as exploratory: path voting's value depends on the task, the predictor, and the distinction between question budgets and actual query costs. What companion implementation does the paper report? A companion Newton boosting implementation provides preliminary full-feature synthetic results, while the main exploratory claims rest on the forest acquisition experiments. live_web_research.snippet: Key Contributions Proposed JevForest, a novel feature acquisition policy using path-dependent proposals from bootstrapped trees, and evaluated its effectiveness across various datasets and acquisition budgets.
live_web_research.page_text: JevForest: Path Voting for Budgeted Feature Acquisition | Arxiv - DeepPaper JevForest: Path Voting for Budgeted Feature Acquisition PDF DeepRead Key Contributions Proposed JevForest, a novel feature acquisition policy using path-dependent proposals from bootstrapped trees, and evaluated its effectiveness across various datasets and acquisition budgets. Abstract Choosing which information to observe is central to prediction under limited observation budgets. We study JevForest, a feature acquisition policy that aggregates path-dependent proposals from bootstrapped trees, weights them by global training information gain, and predicts from the acquired values with a shared masked classifier. An online implementation queries Jev for semantic answers selected by this policy. On small balanced held-out samples, four-question forest acquisition achieves accuracy $0.729$ on AG News ($n=48$), compared with $0.667$ for a static gain ranking and $0.583$ for random ordering. On TREC ($n=24$), the ordering reverses: forest accuracy is $0.667$, compared with $0.750$ and $0.833$. Asking all eight questions in one batch yields higher accuracy at lower measured cost and latency than four sequential forest queries; direct Jev classification matches the batch accuracy while costing less. Offline MiniBooNE experiments yield accuracy $0.845\pm0.010$ at ten features and $0.885\pm0.008$ at forty features over three jointly varying data and forest seeds (mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation). A companion Newton boosting implementation provides preliminary full-feature synthetic results. These exploratory findings establish a working Jev acquisition workflow but do not support a general advantage for path voting: its value depends on the task, predictor, and the distinction between question budgets and actual query costs. Summary JevForest introduces a path-voting mechanism for budgeted feature acquisition, demonstrating task-dependent performance improvements in sequential and batch information gathering. article.body:
JevForest paper reports exploratory feature-acquisition tests

Yu Yan’s JevForest paper proposes a policy that uses bootstrapped-tree proposals to select features under limited observation budgets. Its online implementation queries Jev for selected semantic answers. In small tests, four-question acquisition outperformed static and random ordering on AG News, but not TREC. The paper account identifies no buyer, payment, contract or revenue stream; it establishes no commercial transaction.
